This week

8-week arrest-lead programme

What changed in the 2025 guidelines
  • IV first (AHA 1); IO if IV fails (AHA 2a; ERC: after 2 attempts); central access only by trained hands if both fail (AHA 2b). Endotracheal drugs removed.
  • Adrenaline as early as possible in non-shockable rhythms; in shockable rhythms after the 2nd shock (AHA) or the 3rd (ERC).
  • Persistent VF/pVT (≥3 shocks): optimise basics. ERC: consider an antero-posterior vector change; DSED not routine · AHA: usefulness of vector change and DSED not established (2b).
  • Calcium, bicarbonate, steroids: not routine; only for a specific indication (ERC: do not routinely give calcium).
  • POCUS only by experienced hands, never at the cost of compressions, never the sole reason to stop.
  • Physiology-guided CPR (ERC): EtCO₂ ≥25 mmHg and diastolic ≥30 mmHg with an arterial line; 50–100 µg adrenaline boluses then.
  • Cardioversion: AF ≥200 J (AHA) / maximum (ERC); flutter 200 J (AHA) / 70–120 J (ERC). Stable wide-complex: AHA: procainamide, amiodarone or sotalol may be considered (2b; the chart shows procainamide and amiodarone).
  • Post-ROSC: temperature control 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 h (AHA) / no fever ≤37.5 °C for at least 72 h (ERC); MAP ≥65; SpO₂ 90–98 % (AHA) / 94–98 % (ERC); normocapnia; emergent angiography for ST-elevation, without it only for selected patients (shock, VT/VF, ongoing ischaemia); prognosticate ≥72 h after ROSC (ERC) / after normothermia (AHA), multimodally.
  • Heat stroke: cool at once, ice-water immersion at ≥0.15 °C/min (AHA), the fastest method available (ERC); stop at 38.5–39 °C; no antipyretics.
  • Choking (AHA 2025): alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts in adults (ERC: the same sequence).

AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC 2025 · ERC Guidelines 2025 (ALS, post-resuscitation care, special circumstances) · ILCOR CoSTR 2025 · Rosen's Emergency Medicine 10th ed. for the case bank. A training tool: follow your institution's protocol.

Lead a code

Each scenario starts before the arrest. Recognise and treat the cause and you may prevent it; miss it and the patient arrests on a cause-specific rhythm. Random cases never show the cause: as in the ER, the story unfolds only through what you ask, examine and order, and you commit a working diagnosis when you have one.
